metadata.title: Prognostic Value of Impaired Vocal Cord Mobility in T2N0 Glottic Cancer Treated With IMRT

sections.text: ABSTRACT Objectives To evaluate the prognostic importance of impaired vocal cord mobility (VCM) in T2N0 glottic cancer. Methods All patients with T2N0 glottic cancer treated with partial laryngeal IMRT in 2009–2021 in our institution were retrospectively reviewed. For comparison, cohorts with T1N0 and T3N0 disease were also included. Locoregional failure (LRF), disease‐free survival (DFS), and overall survival (OS) were compared among T1N0, T2N0 with normal VCM (T2‐Normal‐VCM), T2N0 with impaired VCM (T2‐Impaired‐VCM), and T3N0 groups. Multivariable analysis (MVA) assessed the prognostic value of VCM within the T2N0 group. Results A total of 642 cases were included: 288 T1N0, 224 T2N0 (147 T2‐Normal‐VCM, 77 T2‐Impaired‐VCM), and 130 T3N0. Median follow‐up was 5.0 years (IQR 3.4–6.2). Five‐year LRF for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 were 4% (95% CI 2–6), 9% (5–15), 27% (17–38), and 35% (27–44), respectively. Corresponding DFS was 83% (78–88), 80% (73–87), 55% (45–68), and 50% (41–60), while OS was 85% (80–90), 86% (80–92), 71% (61–83), and 59% (50–69), respectively. In T2N0, MVA confirmed that impaired VCM was associated with higher LRF (aHR 3.72 [95% CI 1.79–7.71], p < 0.001), lower DFS (aHR 2.74 [1.68–4.45], p < 0.001), and lower OS (aHR 2.07 [1.17–3.67], p = 0.013). Conclusions In this contemporary cohort, LRF rates increased stepwise from T1N0 to T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 glottic cancer. Within T2N0 disease, impaired VCM is an adverse prognostic factor, supporting subdivision into T2a (normal VCM) and T2b (impaired VCM) in future TNM revisions. Prospective studies are warranted to assess whether treatment intensification can improve outcomes for T2‐Impaired‐VCM disease. Level of Evidence 3.

Laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancer are the only head and neck cancers (HNCs) in which a functional variable, “vocal cord mobility” (VCM), is included as a cT category modifier in the UICC/AJCC TNM classification. In TNM8, glottic cancer is classified as T2 if there is supraglottic extension, subglottic extension, or impaired VCM, without further subdivision. However, several studies suggest these three T2 modifiers do not share equal prognostic weight, with impaired VCM potentially conferring a higher risk of disease recurrence than supraglottic or subglottic extension alone [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ]. The association between impaired VCM and reduced local control (LC) in T2 glottic cancer was first reported in 1967 [ 9 ]. The RTOG 9512 trial further subdivided T2 glottic cancers with normal VCM as “T2a” and impaired VCM as “T2b” and demonstrated inferior locoregional control in the “T2b” group. However, this subdivision has never been formally incorporated into the UICC/AJCC TNM classification. A meta‐analysis of 21 retrospective studies confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of impaired VCM in T2 disease [ 10 ]. A retrospective analysis of T2 glottic cancer cases treated between 1986 and 2013 at the Cleveland Clinic also demonstrated inferior LC with radiotherapy alone in patients with impaired VCM, suggesting that these patients might benefit from the addition of chemotherapy, similar to T3N0 disease [ 5 ]. Most patients in these studies were treated before the widespread adoption of IMRT [ 5 , 10 ], so the impact of modern techniques like IMRT with daily cone‐beam image guidance (IGRT) was not evaluated. Furthermore, dose and fractionation intensification, such as moderately accelerated schedules (e.g., six fractions per week), have improved LC and may reduce outcome differences between T2 tumors with impaired versus normal VCM [ 11 ]. Reappraising the prognostic significance of impaired VCM in a contemporary precision‐radiotherapy cohort is therefore warranted given its potential therapeutic implications. Our institution introduced partial laryngeal IMRT with daily laryngeal soft tissue IGRT from mid‐2008 for both T1N0 and T2N0 glottic cancers [ 11 ]. This provides an opportunity to reappraise the impact of impaired VCM in this group of contemporaneously treated patients. To appreciate whether the stepwise risk increment with higher T categories within T1–T3N0 still exists after stratifying T2 into normal VCM vs. impaired VCM, we also included T1N0 and T3N0 glottic cancer patients treated in the same period for comparison.

This retrospective study was approved by the institutional ethics review board with waiver for individual patient consent. All patients with T1‐3N0M0 glottic cancer treated with partial laryngeal IMRT between January 1, 2009, and December 31, 2021, were identified from the institutional HNC Bio‐clinical Anthology of Outcomes System, which prospectively registers and records baseline and outcome data for all newly diagnosed HNC patients referred to our institution [ 12 ]. The presence or absence of the three cT2‐defining features was further specified: supraglottic extension, subglottic extension, and/or impaired VCM.

All patients were assessed and treated by a multidisciplinary HNC team, according to institutional IG‐IMRT protocols, i.e., with definitive partial laryngeal IMRT, asymmetric PTV margins (5 mm radial and 1 cm superior and inferior expansion), and daily CBCT matching to laryngeal soft tissue. Non‐bulky T1a glottic cancer received 51 Gy/20f/4w (5f/w). Prior to 2010, T1b or T2 glottic cancers were treated with a hypofractionated radiotherapy regimen (60 Gy/25f/5w, 5f/w). After 2010, moderately accelerated (6f/w) radiotherapy regimens were preferred for most T2 glottic cancers, delivering 70 Gy/35f/6w (6f/w), reflecting recognition of a more adverse prognosis for T2 compared to T1 disease in our environment and the need for treatment intensification [ 13 ]. Exceptions included T1b or early T2 (involving < 5 mm of subglottis or ventricle, without false cord involvement and with normal VCM), which were treated to 66 Gy/33f/5.5w (6f/w) [ 11 ]. Occasionally, elderly patients or those preferring shorter course IMRT received hypofractionated IMRT using 60 Gy/25f/5w (5f/w). Patients with T3N0 glottic cancer received concurrent chemoradiotherapy, except when contraindicated due to medical reasons, anticipated intolerance to chemotherapy or patient preference [ 14 ]. Chemotherapy consisted of cisplatin administered either tri‐weekly 100 mg/m 2 or weekly 40 mg/m 2 , delivered concurrently with IMRT (70 Gy/35f/7w, 5f/w). For T3N0 glottic patients unable to receive chemotherapy, altered fractionation radiotherapy was delivered as follows: (a) moderately accelerated radiotherapy (preferred): 70 Gy in 35 fractions over 6 weeks, 70 Gy/35f/6w; (b) hypofractionated radiotherapy (for selected frail elderly patients): 60 Gy/25f/5w; or (c) hyperfractionated accelerated radiotherapy (for very bulky disease): 64 Gy/40f/4w (1.6 Gy/f, twice‐daily, 10f/w). Almost all T1‐2N0 glottic cancer patients were treated with partial laryngeal IMRT to the primary site only, without elective neck irradiation (ENI), except when lymph nodes were suspicious or indeterminate. T3N0 disease received IMRT to the primary site plus bilateral ENI of levels II–IV. The radiotherapy target delineation was described previously [ 11 ]. The precision of treatment delivery was ensured with daily cone‐beam CT matching to laryngeal soft tissue for T1‐2N0 glottic cancer. For T3N0 glottic cancer, IGRT was matched to cervical vertebrae bone while ensuring laryngeal soft tissue was within the PTV. Treatment response was evaluated 3 months after radiotherapy using imaging and clinical assessment. Ongoing surveillance was performed in a multidisciplinary clinic through physical examination and endoscopy, with or without imaging of the head, neck, or thorax. The typical follow‐up schedule was every 3 months for the first 2 years, every 4–6 months in year 3, and every 6 months until year 5. Local failure (LF), defined as persistent or recurrent disease after radiotherapy, was confirmed by biopsy whenever feasible. Distant metastases were primarily diagnosed based on unequivocal radiologic evidence, with pathological confirmation when possible.

Descriptive statistics summarized clinical characteristics, with categorical variables compared using the chi‐square or Fisher's exact test and continuous variables compared using the Student's t ‐test within the T2N0 cohort stratified by VCM. Time‐to‐event outcomes were measured from the date of radiotherapy initiation and compared with log‐rank tests among the following 4 cohorts: T1N0, T2N0 with normal VCM (T2‐Normal‐VCM), T2N0 with impaired VCM (T2‐Impaired VCM), and T3N0. Actuarial rates of LF, regional failure (RF), locoregional failure (LRF), and distant failure (DF) were calculated using competing‐risk method with death without corresponding event of interest as a competing event. Actuarial rates of overall survival (OS) and disease‐free survival (DFS) were estimated with the Kaplan–Meier method. Events for DFS included death, LF, RF, or DF, whichever occurred first. Within the T2N0 cohort, multivariable analyses (MVAs) were used to assess the prognostic impact of impaired VCM on DFS, OS, and LRF, adjusting for age, ECOG performance status, smoking status, and radiotherapy regimen. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (two‐tailed).

A total of 642 patients were eligible: 288 T1N0, 147 T2‐Normal‐VCM, 77 T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and 130 T3N0. A total of 1/288 (0.3%) T1N0, 10/147 (7%) T2‐Normal‐VCM, 6/77 (8%) T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and 129/130 (99%) T3N0 received bilateral ENI, while one elderly (88‐year‐old) patient with T3N0 glottic cancer only received ipsilateral ENI to minimize toxicity. Details of the entire cohort are presented in Table S1 . Within the T2N0 group, the T2‐Impaired‐VCM subset had a lower rate of subglottic extension than T2‐Normal‐VCM (40% vs. 60%, p = 0.003), but similar gross tumor volume (GTV), derived from peer‐reviewed contours within the radiation plan (median 3.0 vs. 2.6 cc, p = 0.11) and anterior commissure involvement (64% vs. 66%, p = 0.93). More T2‐Impaired‐VCM patients received the 70 Gy/35f/6w regimen (65% vs. 50%, p = 0.005) (Table 1 ). Table S2 shows the distribution of supraglottic and subglottic extension within the two VCM subsets.

After a median follow‐up time of 5.0 (IQR, 3.4–6.2) years, there were 148 deaths, 77 LF, 14 RF, and 25 DF in the entire cohort. Actuarial 5‐year rates for OS, DFS, LF, RF, LRF, and DF for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 disease are provided in Table 2 . The 5‐year OS rates for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 disease were 85% (95% CI, 80–90), 86% (95% CI, 80–92), 71% (95% CI, 61–83), and 59% (95% CI, 50–69), respectively ( p < 0.001) (Figure 1A ). The corresponding 5‐year DFS rates were 83% (95% CI, 78–88), 80% (95% CI, 73–87), 55% (95% CI, 45–68), and 50% (95% CI, 41–60), respectively ( p < 0.001) (Figure 1B ). Compared to T2‐Normal‐VCM, the T2‐Impaired‐VCM subset had significantly lower DFS (55% vs. 80%, p < 0.001) and OS (71% vs. 86%, p = 0.001). LF occurred in 9 T1N0, 10 T2‐Normal‐VCM, 17 T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and 41 T3N0 cases. Table S3 shows LF frequency by the radiotherapy regimen. The 5‐year LF rates for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 disease were 3% (95% CI, 2–6), 8% (95% CI, 4–13), 20% (95% CI, 12–30), and 35% (95% CI, 27–44), respectively ( p < 0.001) (Figure 2A ). LF was significantly higher in the T2‐Impaired‐VCM vs. T2‐Normal‐VCM subset (20% vs. 8%, p = 0.002). RF occurred in 1 T1N0, 4 T2‐Normal‐VCM, 5 T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and 4 T3N0 cases, of which 8 were isolated RFs without LF: 1 T1N0, 2 T2‐Normal‐VCM (1 with both supra−/sub‐glottic extension; 1 with supraglottic extension), and 5 T2‐Impaired‐VCM (all 5 with sub‐glottic extension). Notably, of the 17 T1‐2N0 cases treated with bilateral ENI, 2 experienced RF within the ENI volumes (1 T1N0 and 1 T2‐Impaired‐VCM). The 5‐year RF rates for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 were 0% (95% CI, 0–2), 3% (95% CI, 1–8), 7% (95% CI, 2–14), and 3% (95% CI, 1–8), respectively ( p = 0.009) (Figure 2B ). There was no significant difference in RF between T2‐Impaired‐VCM vs. T2‐Normal‐VCM (7% vs. 3%, p = 0.196). The 5‐year LRF rates for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 were 4% (95% CI, 2–6), 9% (95% CI, 5–15), 27% (95% CI, 17–38), and 35% (95% CI, 27–44), respectively ( p < 0.001) (Figure 2C ). LRF was much higher in the T2‐Impaired‐VCM vs. T2‐Normal‐VCM subset (27% vs. 9%, p < 0.001). Of the 25 patients who developed distant metastases, 18 were lung metastases. The 5‐year DF rates for T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 disease were 1% (95% CI, 0–2), 2% (95% CI, 0–6), 7% (95% CI, 3–14), and 14% (95% CI, 8–21), respectively ( p < 0.001) (Figure 2D ). DF was numerically higher in T2‐Impaired‐VCM vs. T2‐Normal‐VCM (7% vs. 2% at 5 years) but did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.052).

Within the T2N0 glottic cancer cohort, MVA confirmed that patients with impaired VCM had significantly worse outcomes, with an adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 2.07 (95% CI, 1.17–3.67; p = 0.013) for OS, 2.74 (95% CI, 1.68–4.45; p < 0.001) for DFS, and 3.72 (95% CI, 1.79–7.71; p < 0.001) for LRF compared with those with normal VCM (Table 3 ). MVA for DF was not performed due to the insufficient number of events (DF only occurred in 7 T2N0 patients: 2 with normal VCM and 5 with impaired VCM). Poor performance status (ECOG 2–4) was also associated with inferior OS (aHR, 3.51; 95% CI, 1.51–8.18; p = 0.004) and DFS (aHR, 3.00; 95% CI, 1.31–6.87; p = 0.010), while increasing age was linked to worse OS (aHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03–1.10; p < 0.001) and DFS (aHR, 1.03; 95% CI, 1.00–1.06; p = 0.025). Smoking status and radiotherapy regimen were not significantly associated with OS, DFS, or LRF on MVA.

In this large contemporary cohort of T1‐3N0 glottic carcinoma treated with partial laryngeal IMRT, we confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of impaired VCM in T2N0 disease. Patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM had significantly worse OS, DFS, and higher LRF than those with T2‐Normal‐VCM, yet outcomes remained superior to T3N0. These findings provide strong evidence supporting subdivision of T2 into “T2a” (supraglottic or subglottic extension with normal VCM) and “T2b” (impaired VCM) in future TNM staging iterations, given the implications for treatment intensity including the potential use of concurrent chemotherapy. Impaired VCM may reflect subclinical paraglottic extension and/or deep tumor infiltration of the thyroarytenoid muscle and surrounding tissues that are not readily detected by conventional imaging [ 15 ], indicating more advanced disease than initially appreciated on clinic‐radiological assessment [ 16 ]. This deeper involvement may promote hypoxia‐induced radioresistance, providing a plausible biological rationale for worse LC despite comparable radiation doses [ 17 ]. As several studies have also reported inferior outcomes after laser surgery alone [ 6 , 18 , 19 ], this effect appears largely independent of treatment modality. Several treatment intensification strategies could be considered to improve outcomes for T2‐Impaired‐VCM, such as altered fractionation with a higher biologically effective dose (BED 10 ) or the addition of concurrent chemotherapy. Current guidelines have not recommended chemoradiotherapy for T2N0 glottic cancer [ 20 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests its potential benefit for the T2‐Impaired‐VCM subset. Several retrospective studies have reported improved LRC with chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy alone in T2N0 disease with high‐risk features, including impaired VCM [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ]. A recent Egyptian randomized trial enrolled 62 patients with unfavorable T2 glottic cancer (53 patients had impaired VCM) to receive either radiotherapy alone (65.25 Gy in 29 fractions) or concurrent chemoradiotherapy (65.25 Gy in 29 fractions with weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m 2 or carboplatin AUC2) between 2019 and 2023 [ 26 ]. After a median follow‐up of 42 months, the chemoradiotherapy group achieved higher LC (90.6% versus 63.3%, p = 0.016), 3‐year local progression‐free survival (85.5% vs. 57.8%, p = 0.015) and a numerically higher 3‐year OS (93.2% vs. 77.1%, p = 0.063). Given these findings, concurrent chemoradiotherapy is a promising option for T2‐Impaired‐VCM, pending confirmation in future trials. In theory, outcomes might also be improved by modifying the radiotherapy regimen through dose escalation or accelerated fractionation. However, radiotherapy intensification has shown limited success in this setting. In our cohort, patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM treated with a higher BED 10 regimen (accelerated regimen, 70 Gy/35f/6 weeks) had a numerically lower LF rate (22% vs. 32%) than those who received a lower BED 10 regimen (60 Gy/25f/5 weeks, Table S2 ), although the MVA did not reach statistical significance (aHR 1.71, p = 0.14), likely due to the small sample size. Similarly, the randomized RTOG 9512 trial compared hyperfractionated (79.2 Gy/66f, 1.2 Gy/f, twice‐daily) vs. conventionally fractionated radiotherapy (70 Gy/35f/7w) for 250 T2N0 glottic cancer patients, and found only a non‐significant trend toward modest improvement (8%) with hyperfractionation overall, and no apparent benefit in the T2‐Impaired‐VCM subgroup [ 27 ]. These findings parallel the benefit of hyperfractionated radiotherapy shown in the MARCH meta‐analysis for HNC (a much larger dataset exceeding 11,000 compared to the RTOG 9512 trial comprising 250 cases), suggesting the RTOG 9512 results were underpowered yet consistent with expectations [ 27 , 28 ]. Taken together, and considering that altered fractionation was already employed in our cohort, fractionation modifications alone are unlikely to equalize outcomes between T2‐Impaired‐VCM and T2‐Normal‐VCM. We observed a 5‐year RF rate of 7% (95% CI, 2–14) in patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM, which was numerically higher than in T3N0 disease (3%; 95% CI, 1–8). The lower rate in T3N0 likely reflects the routine use of ENI in these patients. Nevertheless, the 7% rate remains below the threshold at which most clinicians would advocate for ENI in all patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM. In fact, of the 17 T1‐2N0 cases treated with bilateral ENI, RF still occurred in 2 patients (1 T1N0 and 1 T2‐Impaired‐VCM) within ENI volumes, suggesting intrinsic variation in tumor biology might play a role. Schrijvers et al. performed immunohistochemistry for HIF1a, CA‐IX, and GLUT‐1 on 91 glottic cancer specimens, and reported that tumor with overexpression of HIF1a or CA‐IX portends worse LC than those with low expression [ 17 ]. Other series have also reported somewhat increased RF rates (7%–15% [ 3 , 29 , 30 ]) in patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM. The above mentioned randomized trial from Egypt performed ENI to bilateral level II‐IV for all patients treated with chemoradiotherapy, and there was no isolated RF in this arm [ 26 ]. On the other hand, our results confirm that omission of ENI seems to be safe in patients with T1 and T2‐Normal‐VCM disease, with 5‐year LF rates of 0% and 3%, respectively. This again demonstrates that the reduced dose to the anterior level III by using IMRT compared with lateral‐opposed fields does not result in high rates of RFs for these early‐stage glottic cancers, which was also confirmed in a recent meta‐analysis [ 31 ]. However, among the 30 patients with both T2‐Impaired‐VCM and subglottic extension, 5 (16.7%) developed isolated RFs, suggesting that this subgroup might warrant consideration of ENI to bilateral levels II–IV, although our sample size is limited. Differential outcomes after salvage surgery in T2 glottic carcinoma according to VCM are well documented, with consistently better results in T2‐Normal‐VCM than T2‐Impaired‐VCM disease [ 3 ]. Kaplan et al. reported successful salvage surgery in 70% of T2‐Normal‐VCM versus 11% of T2‐Impaired‐VCM tumors [ 32 ], while other series have also reported higher post‐salvage LC for T2‐Normal‐VCM (81%–83%) compared with T2‐Impaired‐VCM (67%–68%) [ 30 , 33 ]. Close surveillance during the first 3 years is therefore especially important for patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM to enable early detection and timely salvage intervention. A major challenge for subdividing T2a (normal VCM) and T2b (impaired VCM) is the lack of objective criteria for evaluating VCM, which may lead to variability in classifying T2 lesions both across institutions and within the same institution over time [ 34 ]. Misclassification of a T2‐Impaired‐VCM as T2‐Normal‐VCM could especially result in substantial undertreatment, particularly if institutions choose to apply concurrent chemoradiotherapy only in patients with T2‐Impaired‐VCM. It should be noted that, according to the UICC/AJCC staging principles, if there is uncertainty in assigning a subcategory, the patient should be assigned to the general category [ 35 ]. Although a recent study showed only a modest (67.7%) inter‐rater agreement with a five‐category VCM scale, it reassuringly improved to 91.4% when using a three‐category scale (normal/impaired/fixed) for VCM [ 36 ]. Although this study presents a comprehensive analysis with a large cohort treated consistently with partial laryngeal IMRT, several limitations should be acknowledged. While clinical parameters were captured prospectively at the point of care, the retrospective study design required reliance on clinician documentation for assessment of VCM. The T2 cohort was limited to patients treated with radiotherapy alone, which may reduce applicability to those managed with primary surgery. Additionally, we did not evaluate the impact of impaired VCM on post‐radiotherapy voice quality, an important aspect of survivorship and quality of life. Nonetheless, impaired VCM has been reported as an adverse prognostic factor for voice outcomes following both surgery and radiotherapy in other studies [ 6 , 37 ].

Our study demonstrated that impaired VCM is an independent prognostic factor in T2N0 glottic cancer and is associated with a higher LRF rate. A stepwise increase in LRF risk was observed across T1N0, T2‐Normal‐VCM, T2‐Impaired‐VCM, and T3N0 disease. These findings support subdividing T2 into T2a (normal VCM) and T2b (impaired VCM) in future TNM classification updates. Further studies are warranted to assess whether treatment intensification, such as concurrent chemotherapy, could improve outcomes in T2N0 glottic cancer patients with impaired VCM.
